lede: A straight line has one gradient everywhere; a curve's gradient changes from point to point. The gradient of the tangent at a point, the straight line that runs along the curve there, is how fast the quantity is changing at that moment: its instantaneous rate of change.
can: Draw a tangent at a stated point and find its gradient from two far-apart points on it.
Tell an average rate over an interval (a chord) from a rate at one instant (a tangent).
Give a rate with its units and its sign, and say what it means in the story.

caption: The curve gets steeper, so her speed keeps changing; the tangent at P runs along the curve there.

md: A cyclist's distance-time graph curves upwards: she is speeding up, so her speed is different at every moment. Her speed at one instant is the gradient of the tangent there, the straight line that touches the curve at that point and runs along it. Read two points on the tangent and work out rise over run. On a straight line you read the gradient once; on a curve you choose the moment first.

stem: The tangent to the cyclist's graph at $P$, where $t = 4$, passes through $(2, 0)$ and $(8, 24)$. Estimate her speed at $t = 4$ s.

steps.decision: Read both points from the axes; the vertical axis is in metres.
The horizontal axis is in seconds.

steps.working: Gradient $= 24 \div 6 = 4$, so her speed at $t = 4$ is about $4$ m/s
steps.decision: Metres over seconds: the units come off the axes.

prompt: A tangent to a distance-time graph, in metres and seconds, passes through $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 20)$. What speed does it give?
explain: Rise $= 20 - 2 = 18$ m and run $= 5 - 1 = 4$ s, so the gradient is $18 \div 4 = 4.5$ m/s.

twin.prompt: A tangent to a distance-time graph, in metres and seconds, passes through $(2, 3)$ and $(7, 33)$. What speed does it give?
twin.explain: Rise $= 33 - 3 = 30$ m, run $= 7 - 2 = 5$ s, so the gradient is $30 \div 5 = 6$ m/s.

optionNotes.why: 33 is a distance read off the line, not a rate.
$33 \div 7$ joins the origin to a point: a chord, so an average.
Run over rise turns the gradient upside down.
20 is how far she has gone at that point, a value on the tangent, not how fast the distance is changing.
$20 \div 5$ is the gradient of a chord from the origin, an average since the start.
That is run over rise; a gradient is rise over run.

text: Why the tangent gives the instant rate

md: An average speed over an interval is the gradient of a chord: change in distance over change in time. Shrink the interval towards one moment and the chord swings round until it lies along the tangent. So the tangent's gradient is where those averages end up: the speed at that instant. You never need the chords in an exam, but they are why the method works.

stem: On the cyclist's graph, chords from $P$ at $t = 4$ run to $t = 8$, $t = 6$ and $t = 5$. What do their gradients approach?

steps.decision: The average speed over four seconds.
A shorter interval, a smaller average: she was slower at the start of it.
Shorter again.

steps.working: The averages close in on $4$ m/s, the gradient of the tangent at $P$
steps.decision: Each shorter interval is a better average for the one moment; the tangent is where they end up.

prompt: Chords from the point where $t = 3$ on a curve have gradients $9$, $7.5$, $6.6$ and $6.3$ as the other end closes in. What is the gradient of the tangent at $t = 3$?
explain: The chords' gradients fall towards 6 as the interval shrinks, so the tangent, where they end up, has gradient about 6.

twin.prompt: Chords from the point where $t = 1$ on a curve have gradients $2.2$, $1.6$, $1.3$ and $1.1$ as the other end closes in. What is the gradient of the tangent at $t = 1$?
twin.explain: The gradients fall towards 1 as the chord shrinks, so the tangent at $t = 1$ has gradient about 1.

optionNotes.why: 2.2 belongs to the longest chord, the furthest from the tangent.
The mean of the four is not their limit; they fall towards 1.
The chords are not flattening to 0; they settle near 1.
9 is the gradient of the longest chord, the roughest average of all.
Averaging the chords' gradients does not find where they are heading; they head for 6.
The chords all slope upwards, so the tangent is not flat.

text: Chord or tangent: read the question

md: Two questions, two lines. *Over* an interval asks for an average: draw the chord joining its two ends. *At* or *when* asks for one instant: draw the tangent there. On a curve that bends, the two answers differ, so the wording decides which line you draw. Underline the words that name the time before you pick up the ruler.

caption: The chord gives the average rate over the 10 minutes; the tangent gives the rate at t = 8.

stem: A tank fills with water. From its graph, $V = 0$ at $t = 0$ and $V = 200$ at $t = 10$ minutes, and the tangent at $t = 8$ passes through $(0, 128)$ and $(10, 208)$. Find the average rate over the first 10 minutes and the rate at $t = 8$.

steps.decision: 'Over the first 10 minutes': a chord from end to end.
'At $t = 8$': the tangent there.

steps.working: $8$ is well below $20$: the filling is slowing down
steps.decision: The curve flattens, so the rate late on is less than the average.

prompt: A part asks for the average rate of growth over the first 6 hours. Which line do you draw?
explain: 'Over the first 6 hours' is an interval, so the average rate is the gradient of the chord joining its two ends.

twin.prompt: A part asks for the rate of cooling when $t = 9$ minutes. Which line do you draw?
twin.explain: 'When $t = 9$' names one instant, so the rate is the gradient of the tangent at that point.

optionNotes.why: A chord gives an average over nine minutes, but 'when' asks for one instant.
A vertical line has no gradient; the instant needs a tangent.
Even a short chord is an average over two minutes, not the rate at $t = 9$.
A tangent gives the rate at one instant, but 'over the first 6 hours' asks for an average.
A tangent at the middle still measures one moment, not the whole interval.
A vertical line has no gradient to read; the rate needs a chord.

text: Average or end: which is bigger?

md: On a curve that gets steeper, the rate at the end of an interval is bigger than the average across it, because the average includes the flatter start. On a curve that flattens, the end rate is the smaller. Saying which, and why, is a common one-mark part.

stem: On the cyclist's graph, $d = 32$ m at $t = 8$ s, and the tangent there has gradient $8$. Compare her average speed over the 8 seconds with her speed at $t = 8$.

steps.decision: The chord from the origin to the end.

steps.working: At $t = 8$: about $8$ m/s, from the tangent
steps.decision: The rate at the last instant.

steps.working: $8 > 4$, because the curve gets steeper: she is speeding up
steps.decision: The average is pulled down by the slow start.

prompt: A curve gets flatter across an interval. How does the rate at the end compare with the average rate over the interval?
options: The rate at the end is smaller
The rate at the end is larger
The rate at the end is zero
answer: The rate at the end is smaller
explain: A flattening curve is steepest at the start, so the average includes steeper stretches than the end has: the end rate is the smaller.

options: The rate at the end is larger
The rate at the end is smaller
The rate at the end is zero
twin.answer: The rate at the end is larger
twin.explain: A steepening curve is steepest at the end, while the average includes the flatter start, so the end rate is the larger.

optionNotes.option: The rate at the end is smaller
optionNotes.why: A steepening curve is steepest at the end, so the end rate is the larger.
They are equal only on a straight line.

optionNotes.option: The rate at the end is zero
optionNotes.why: A steepening curve does not end flat.

optionNotes.option: The rate at the end is larger
optionNotes.why: A flattening curve is steepest at the start, so its end rate is below the average, not above it.
The two are equal only when the gradient is the same all along, as on a straight line.

optionNotes.option: The rate at the end is zero
optionNotes.why: The rate at the end is small, but it is zero only where the tangent is flat.

steps.decision: A line that cuts the curve twice is a chord, which measures an average.

prompt: A tangent has been drawn at $t = 5$. Which two points give the most reliable gradient?
options: Two points on the tangent, far apart
Two points on the curve, either side of $t = 5$
Two points on the tangent, close together
The point of contact and the origin
answer: Two points on the tangent, far apart
explain: Only the tangent has the curve's direction at $t = 5$, and points far apart along it keep a small reading slip from mattering.

twin.prompt: Why is a tangent drawn long rather than short?
options: So the two points read from it can be far apart
So that it reaches both axes
So that it crosses the curve twice
Because a short line cannot be a tangent
twin.answer: So the two points read from it can be far apart
twin.explain: A long line lets you read two points a long way apart, so a small misreading changes the gradient very little.

optionNotes.option: So that it reaches both axes
optionNotes.why: Reaching the axes is not the aim; far-apart points are.

optionNotes.option: So that it crosses the curve twice
optionNotes.why: A line that crosses the curve twice is a chord.

optionNotes.option: Because a short line cannot be a tangent
optionNotes.why: A short line can still be a tangent; it is just harder to read accurately.

optionNotes.option: Two points on the curve, either side of $t = 5$
optionNotes.why: Two points on the curve make a chord, which gives an average, not the rate at $t = 5$.

optionNotes.option: Two points on the tangent, close together
optionNotes.why: Close points turn a small reading slip into a large error in the gradient.

optionNotes.option: The point of contact and the origin
optionNotes.why: The line from the origin to the contact point is a chord from the start.

text: The units come off the axes

md: A gradient is a rate, and its unit is the vertical axis's unit over the horizontal axis's. Metres against seconds give m/s, a speed; velocity in m/s against seconds gives m/s², an acceleration; litres against minutes give litres per minute. Read the axis labels before you write the answer. In an interpretation part the units are often worth a mark of their own.

title: Why the units divide
md: A gradient divides a change in the vertical quantity by a change in the horizontal one, so its units divide in the same way: metres by seconds, litres by minutes.

stem: Give the units of the gradient for three graphs.

steps.decision: Metres over seconds: a speed.
Metres per second, per second: an acceleration.

steps.working: Volume (litres) against time (minutes): litres per minute
steps.decision: Always the vertical unit over the horizontal one.

prompt: A graph shows the height of a plant in cm against time in days. What are the units of its gradient?
explain: The vertical unit over the horizontal unit: centimetres per day, the rate the plant grows.

twin.prompt: A graph shows the cost in £ against the mass in kg. What are the units of its gradient?
twin.explain: Pounds over kilograms: the price per kilogram.

optionNotes.why: Kilograms per pound turns the rate upside down.
A price alone is not a rate; it is per kilogram.
Rates divide units rather than multiply them.
That is the horizontal unit over the vertical one, turned upside down.
A height alone is not a rate; the rate is per day.
A rate divides the units; it never multiplies them.

text: The sign says rising or falling

md: A tangent sloping down has a negative gradient, and the minus sign is part of the answer: it says the quantity is falling. 'The rate is $-8$ cm per minute' and 'the depth is falling at 8 cm per minute' say the same thing; a bare 8 says the opposite. On a velocity graph a negative gradient is a deceleration: the vehicle is slowing down.

steps.decision: The line falls, so the rise is negative.
Time always runs forwards.
Centimetres over minutes.

prompt: A tangent to a cooling curve, in °C and minutes, passes through $(0, 70)$ and $(8, 30)$. What does it tell you?
options: The temperature is falling by about 5 °C each minute
The temperature is rising by about 5 °C each minute
The temperature has fallen by 40 °C altogether
answer: The temperature is falling by about 5 °C each minute
explain: Rise $= 30 - 70 = -40$ over a run of 8 minutes gives $-5$ °C per minute: a fall of about 5 °C each minute at that instant.

twin.prompt: A tangent to a depth-time graph, in cm and hours, passes through $(0, 90)$ and $(6, 0)$. What does it tell you?
options: The depth is falling by about 15 cm each hour
The depth is rising by about 15 cm each hour
The depth has fallen by 90 cm altogether
twin.answer: The depth is falling by about 15 cm each hour
twin.explain: Rise $= 0 - 90 = -90$ over 6 hours gives $-15$ cm per hour: the depth is falling about 15 cm each hour.

optionNotes.option: The depth is rising by about 15 cm each hour
optionNotes.why: The line falls, so the depth is falling, not rising.
15 is a rate per hour, not a depth.

optionNotes.option: The depth has fallen by 90 cm altogether
optionNotes.why: 90 cm is the whole fall along the line, not a rate.

optionNotes.option: The temperature is rising by about 5 °C each minute
optionNotes.why: The line falls from 70 to 30, so the gradient is negative: the temperature is falling, not rising.
A gradient is a rate, not a temperature read from the line.

optionNotes.option: The temperature has fallen by 40 °C altogether
optionNotes.why: 40 °C is the whole fall along the line; the rate divides it by the 8 minutes.

md: Squares are only units when one square is one unit on both axes, and on graph paper it rarely is. So count the squares, multiply by what one square is worth on that axis, and only then divide. A rate that looks several times too big or too small is nearly always this slip.

text: Going further: where the rate is zero

md: At the top of a hill or the bottom of a dip the tangent lies flat, so its gradient is 0: at that instant the quantity is not changing. The steepest part of a curve is where the rate is largest. On a height-time graph of a thrown ball, the top of the arc is where it is momentarily still.
Close to a turning point the tangent is nearly flat, so the rate there is small, and it changes sign as the curve passes over the top.

md:
Estimate a rate at an instant from the gradient of the tangent there.
Use a chord for an average over an interval, a tangent for one moment.
Draw the tangent long and read two far-apart points in axis units.
Give the rate its units, vertical over horizontal, and its sign.

Usually the last two marks of a graph question on Paper 2: draw the curve from a formula, read a value, then 'by drawing a suitable line, estimate the rate'. The first mark is for the tangent itself, so draw it even if the reading defeats you; the second is the value with its units. Stuck: draw the tangent and pick two grid points on it.
